steps.title: A sample and its mean
steps.idea: The true mean $a$ of the population is unknown. One sample of $n$ observations gives a point estimate of it: the sample mean $\bar{x}$.

layers.intuition: Each violet dot is one observation. They collapse into their centre of mass: that point is $\bar{x}$. A new sample gives a new $\bar{x}$.
layers.definition: An estimate $\tilde{a}$ is unbiased if $M\tilde{a} = a$ and consistent if $\tilde{a} \to a$ in probability as $n \to \infty$. The sample mean is both.

steps.title: A cloud of estimates
steps.idea: Repeat the experiment many times. Every sample gives its own $\bar{x}$, and the means gather into a cloud around the true $a$. The larger $n$, the tighter the cloud: its spread is $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$.

layers.intuition: Each violet brick is the mean of one whole sample. The cloud is centred on $a$ (no bias), and the ladder below shows the same experiment for $n = 2, 5, 10, 20, 50$: it narrows like $1/\sqrt{n}$.
layers.definition: An estimate is consistent if it converges to the parameter in probability as $n \to \infty$. Here $D\bar{x} = \sigma^2/n \to 0$, so by Chebyshev's inequality $P(|\bar{x} - a| \ge \varepsilon) \le \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n\varepsilon^2} \to 0$.
layers.details: Even for the skewed law the cloud of $\bar{x}$ is close to normal: this is the central limit theorem from lecture 8 at work.

steps.title: Unbiased variance
steps.idea: The same samples feed two formulas for the variance. Dividing by $n$ underestimates $\sigma^2$ on average; dividing by $n - 1$ removes the bias.

layers.intuition: Coral is divisor $n$, cyan is divisor $n - 1$. Both histograms are built from the very same samples, yet the coral mean stops short of the yellow line $\sigma^2$, and the gap is about $\sigma^2/n$.
layers.details: With divisor $n$ the expectation is $\frac{n-1}{n}\sigma^2$: the spread around $\bar{x}$ is smaller than around the true $a$, because $\bar{x}$ is fitted to the same data. Dividing by $n - 1$ cancels that factor.

steps.title: Confidence interval for the mean
steps.idea: Widen the point into an interval that covers the true mean with a stated probability $\gamma$. Its half-width grows with the spread $s$ and shrinks like $1/\sqrt{n}$.

layers.definition: For normal data $\frac{\bar{x} - a}{s/\sqrt{n}}$ has Student's law with $n - 1$ degrees of freedom; $t_{\gamma}$ is its two-sided quantile, so the interval covers $a$ with probability exactly $\gamma$.

steps.title: A wall of intervals
steps.idea: Draw a new sample again and again. Each gives its own interval; some miss the true mean $a$ and turn coral. The share that covers $a$ settles near $\gamma$: this is what “confidence” means.

layers.intuition: The interval is random, the mean $a$ is not. “95%” is a promise about the procedure: of many intervals built this way, about 95 in 100 catch $a$.
layers.details: A thousand intervals here use exactly the samples of the Confidence Intervals station with the same seed, $n$ and $\gamma$, so the two coverage counts agree to the last interval.

steps.title: When the promise breaks
steps.idea: The $t$ interval is exact only for normal data. With a skewed law and a small sample its coverage drops below $\gamma$. The normal quantile $z_{\gamma}$ in place of $t_{\gamma}$ makes small samples worse still.

steps.title: Homogeneity of two series
steps.idea: Two series of trials give frequencies $m_1/n_1$ and $m_2/n_2$. Are they samples of one probability $p$? Pool them and compare the difference with its standard error.
